problemText: Which of the following statements correctly describes what makes a resource renewable or nonrenewable?
choices: A resource is nonrenewable if it is found deep underground where it cannot be easily accessed by people.
A resource is renewable if it comes from plants or animals that are alive and grow in nature.
A resource is renewable if nature replaces it about as fast as, or faster than, people use it.
A resource is nonrenewable if people have already used some of it up and need to keep finding new supplies.
hints: Focus on the comparison between two speeds: how fast nature replaces the resource and how fast people use it.
The definition is about a rate comparison, not about where the resource comes from or how much has been used.

problemText: A geologist explains that coal formed underground over millions of years from buried plant material under heat and pressure. Coal is being mined and burned today at a rate measured in years. Based on these rates, should coal be classified as renewable or nonrenewable, and why?
choices: Renewable, because coal is still forming somewhere underground right now from organic material.
Nonrenewable, because it is found deep underground and takes energy and equipment to remove from the earth.
Renewable, because it comes from material that was once alive and therefore can be naturally replaced.
Nonrenewable, because coal forms far more slowly than the rate at which it is being mined and burned.
hints: Compare the formation rate (millions of years) to the removal rate (years) — which is much faster?
A resource is nonrenewable when nature cannot replace what is used on any timescale that matters to people.

problemText: A forest management company cuts down trees for lumber and immediately plants new seedlings to replace them. The growth rate of the new seedlings is about the same as the rate at which trees are being harvested. How should the timber from this forest be classified?
choices: Renewable, because new trees are being planted to replace the ones cut at about the same rate.
Nonrenewable, because trees take several years to reach full size and require time to become mature lumber.
Nonrenewable, because the company is removing wood and resources from the forest ecosystem.
Renewable, because trees are living organisms that can regrow and reproduce naturally over time.
hints: The key is whether replacement happens at about the same rate as use — do new trees grow about as fast as old ones are cut?
A resource can be renewable even though it is not unlimited, as long as the replacement rate matches or exceeds the use rate.

problemText: A town pumps water from an aquifer that recharges from rainfall at a steady rate of 2 million gallons per year. In Year One, the town uses 2 million gallons per year and the water table stays stable. In Year Two, a drought reduces rainfall, so the recharge rate drops to 1 million gallons per year, but the town still pumps 2 million gallons per year. Explain how the town's water use should be classified in each year.
choices: Both years are renewable, because rain is still recharging the aquifer in both.
Year One is renewable because pumping equals recharge; Year Two is nonrenewable because pumping exceeds recharge.
Both years are nonrenewable, because the aquifer is not infinite.
Year One is nonrenewable because of drought risk; Year Two is renewable because the town has adapted to use less.
hints: In Year One, compare the pumping rate to the recharge rate — are they matched? In Year Two, does the same comparison hold true?
A resource is renewable only when the use rate does not exceed the replacement rate, regardless of what happens in other years.

problemText: A student claims: 'Solar energy is renewable because the sun will eventually burn out billions of years from now, but on any timescale that matters to people, the sun keeps supplying sunlight at the same rate.' Which part of this statement is correct reasoning, and which part misunderstands what 'renewable' means?
choices: The entire statement is correct; solar energy is renewable for all practical purposes because humans depend on it.
The claim about billions of years is what makes solar renewable; the 'timescale that matters' reasoning misses the point that renewable means lasting extremely long.

The claim about the sun eventually burning out is correct, but that is not why solar energy is classified as renewable — solar is renewable because the sun's current supply rate does not depend on how much sunlight people capture today.
The statement is wrong because renewable resources must last forever without any possibility of depletion in any time period.
hints: Focus on the comparison between how much sunlight arrives and how much people can use — does using more today reduce how much arrives tomorrow?
Renewable classification is about whether the replacement rate depends on the use rate, not about whether something will eventually run out.

problemText: A mining company extracts copper ore from a deposit that formed over millions of years as mineral-rich fluids slowly deposited minerals in rock. A logging company cuts trees from a forest where new trees naturally regrow over decades. Both companies remove large amounts of their resources every year. A student argues: 'Both the copper ore and the timber are nonrenewable because both are being used faster than any human can live to see them regrow.' Identify the error in this reasoning and explain the correct way to classify each resource.
choices: The student is correct; both should be classified as nonrenewable because the time for replacement exceeds the span of a human lifetime.
The student is wrong because copper ore forms over millions of years while trees regrow over decades, making the absolute timescales very different for each resource type.
The student is wrong because trees are living organisms and copper ore is inorganic material, which determines whether they are renewable based on their physical nature.

The student confuses the timescale of replacement with the rate of replacement relative to use — copper ore is nonrenewable because formation is far slower than mining, while timber can be renewable if trees regrow at about the same rate they are cut, regardless of how long that takes.
hints: The definition of renewable compares two rates: how fast nature replaces the resource and how fast people use it — not how long replacement takes in absolute time.
The critical question for each resource is whether replacement happens at about the same rate as use, not whether humans can live to see the replacement happen.

problemText: Coal forms from ancient plant material that was buried under layers of sediment. In what type of environment did the plant material originally accumulate before it was buried?
choices: In thick layers of sand and gravel deposited by ancient rivers
In ancient shallow seas where marine organisms settled on the sea floor
In cracks in rock near subduction zones where magma was rising
In ancient swamps where dead plant material piled up in wet, low-oxygen ground
hints: Think about what kind of wet environment would have lots of dead plant material piling up.
This environment needed low oxygen so the plant material would not fully rot away.

problemText: A geologist finds a thick layer of sand and gravel underground in a region. Which resource is this geologic feature most likely to support today?
choices: A productive aquifer, because sand and gravel are permeable and let water pass through
Coal deposits, because sand and gravel form from swamp material
Oil and natural gas reserves, because sand layers contain buried marine organisms
Copper ore deposits, because sand is found near plate boundaries
hints: Remember what property of sand and gravel makes them useful for water storage and movement.
A productive aquifer needs a thick layer of permeable sediment that water can move through.

problemText: Two neighboring regions have very different geologic histories. Region X was never covered by an ancient sea, while Region Y was once covered by a shallow ancient sea where marine organisms died and were buried. Based on this difference alone, which resource is Region Y more likely to have?
choices: Coal, because ancient seas deposit thick layers of organic material that can be converted into solid fuel over time
Oil and natural gas, because marine organic material buried in sediment can be converted into these resources
Copper ore, because the chemical environment of ancient seas causes dissolved metals to crystallize into ore deposits in sediment layers
Productive aquifers, because seas deposit thick layers of permeable sand and gravel that can store and transmit groundwater
hints: Oil and natural gas form from a specific kind of organic material in a specific setting.
What environment provides the organic material that becomes oil—swamps or ancient seas?

problemText: The Permian Basin in West Texas and New Mexico holds large reserves of oil and natural gas. For this oil and gas to still be there today instead of having seeped away over millions of years, which two geologic features must both be present in the rock layers?
choices: Two separate sealing layers with no permeable rock between them, because oil cannot move through rock of any kind and needs double protection from escape
A thick layer of ancient swamp material above a layer of solid granite, because plant material must have already been converted to coal before oil can form in the rock below
An impermeable sealing layer above a permeable reservoir layer, because oil and gas need to be trapped and prevented from escaping upward
A copper ore deposit above the oil, because dense mineral deposits block upward movement and prevent petroleum fluids from leaking away over time
hints: Oil and gas can seep upward through permeable rock until they hit something they cannot pass through.
Two features are needed: a layer that lets oil move through it, and a layer that stops the oil from escaping.

problemText: Chile and Peru, along South America's west coast, are among the world's largest copper producers. Explain why a region in the middle of a stable continental plate, far from any plate boundary, would not develop the same kind of copper ore deposits even if it had thick layers of sediment and large amounts of rock.
choices: Because copper ore requires twice as much time to form as other ores, and only plate boundaries have been active long enough
Because copper is heavier than other metals and sinks to the bottom of ancient oceans, so it only forms where marine sediment is present
Because thick sediment layers bury swamp material that becomes coal, and coal prevents copper from forming nearby
Because copper ore forms only where hot, mineral-rich fluids rise from magma near a subduction zone, and the middle of a plate has no subducting plate beneath it to produce that magma
hints: Copper ore deposits form near a specific type of plate boundary where the rock is being melted and fluids are rising.
What geologic process must happen to deliver mineral-rich fluids to the rock where copper ore deposits form?

problemText: A mining company wants to find new coal deposits. They are considering three locations: Location 1 has rock that was once heated and melted near a convergent plate boundary; Location 2 has layers of sediment that contain fossil remains of tiny marine organisms; Location 3 has sediment that includes the compacted remains of ancient plants that accumulated in a swamp before being buried under layers of sediment. Based on the geologic process that forms coal, which location is most likely to have coal deposits, and why would drilling deeper at one of the other locations be a waste of time?
choices: Location 3, because coal requires buried ancient plant material from a swamp; Location 1 would not produce coal no matter how deep you drill because its rock was created by magma, not by the burial and compression of plant material

Location 2, because marine organisms accumulate on the ocean floor and compress into coal over millions of years; Location 3 would not produce coal no matter how deep you drill because swamp environments create peat instead of coal-forming material

Location 1, because convergent plate boundaries bury all types of sediment deep enough to form coal; Location 2 would not produce coal no matter how deep you drill because ocean environments lack the plant material that coal requires

Location 3 if swamp conditions existed long enough, but Location 1 could also form coal if heated by plate motion and Location 2 could form coal if enough time and pressure are applied to marine deposits
hints: Coal forms from one specific type of buried plant material in one specific environment—not from any plant material or any marine material.
Think about what makes Location 3 different from Location 1: what process created the rock at each location, and could the other process produce the same resource?

problemText: A tornado warning is issued for your county, meaning a tornado has been indicated nearby and is expected very soon. What should you do right away?
choices: Wait for news confirmation of tornado formation because warnings are sometimes issued as a precaution and the tornado may not actually develop in your immediate area
Act immediately to move to a safe location, such as a small interior room on the lowest floor away from windows
Gather your family and important documents together while staying in your current location so you are ready to move if the tornado gets closer to your home
Leave your home and drive to a shelter in the next town over to be extra safe from the tornado threat in your county
hints: A warning means the hazard is occurring or expected very soon, not just favorable conditions.
The key word in the question is 'right away' — what kind of action does that signal?

problemText: A forecast track shows a hurricane's center moving directly toward a coastal city, but the shaded cone on the map is very wide. A resident asks, 'If my home is just outside the cone, am I safe?' A forecast cone shows possible locations of the storm's center based on the range of accuracy from past forecasts. Based on what a forecast track actually shows, what is the best answer?
choices: Yes, because the cone shows the exact range of the storm's effects, so anything outside it is unaffected
Yes, because the width of the cone shows how much the forecast might be wrong, so homes just outside cannot be hit
No, because the cone shows only where the storm's center might be, and wind, rain, and storm surge can reach well beyond it
No, because the cone is not drawn to scale and the actual storm is much larger than it appears on the map
hints: The cone marks possible paths of the storm's center — what about the storm's effects beyond that center line?
The cone's width is based on how accurate past forecasts have been — does that tell you the size of the storm or the range of possible paths?

problemText: A county has a history of flooding in the low-lying area near the river, but the neighborhood on the hill two kilometers away has never flooded. A river flood forecast is issued for the county. Why should the hill neighborhood still prepare for possible flooding, even though it has been dry during all past floods? Consider that past experience at a location tells you what has already happened there, but not necessarily what could happen under different conditions.
choices: Because the river's behavior changes over time due to climate patterns and the hill neighborhood may be in a new flood risk zone even if it was safe during the last twenty years of records
Because flooding patterns reverse every decade or two, and it is the hill neighborhood's turn to flood this year
Because the forecast data always overestimates danger at safe locations so residents do not become complacent
Because historical safety at a location is not the same as protection — the neighborhood simply has not yet experienced the exact conditions that could cause it to flood
hints: Past safety at a location shows what has happened, but what does it not guarantee about the future?
What does historical data tell you about a specific place, and what does it not tell you?

problemText: A coastal town's forecast shows a hurricane making direct landfall within one day, with forecasters expecting it to remain a strong hurricane through arrival. The town's historical records show that the last three hurricanes on a similar track each caused major wind damage to buildings throughout the town, but storm surge flooding was severe only in the two-block-wide low-lying waterfront district. The town proposes a mitigation action: reinforcing all buildings across the entire town to withstand stronger winds. Evaluate whether this mitigation action fits the forecast and historical evidence.
choices: No, it does not fit the evidence, because the historical record shows storm surge as a major threat only in one specific area, yet the plan reinforces buildings everywhere instead of targeting flood mitigation in the waterfront district
Yes, it fits the evidence, because three previous hurricanes all caused wind damage across the town, so reinforcing all buildings prevents that documented risk from occurring again in the future

Yes, it fits the evidence, because the forecast predicts a strong hurricane making direct landfall, and wind-resistant buildings provide the most effective protection for coastal towns against the full range of hurricane hazards including surge and wind

No, it does not fit the evidence, because historical records indicate that a strong hurricane always generates widespread flooding throughout the entire landing area, so the town should prioritize evacuation and shelter over reinforcing individual structures
hints: What does the historical pattern show about where the storm surge flooding occurred in past similar storms?
A mitigation action taken 'long before any specific storm is forecast' should address the long-term risks the data points to — where is this town's concentrated risk?

problemText: A hurricane forecast shows a storm weakening from a powerful Category 4 to a weak tropical depression within 24 hours after landfall. Forecasters note that once the storm passes inland, it is expected to slow down and drop very heavy rain for several days in the same inland region. Historical records show that past hurricanes with similar landing tracks have also slowed and stalled, dumping intense rainfall and causing severe flooding in the same inland area for days. The city's preparedness plan is to stock emergency supplies, open the emergency shelter, and prepare evacuation routes for wind damage. When should residents also begin preparing specifically for inland flooding?
choices: Only if another storm is forecast in the next few days, because a weakening hurricane forecast means overall threat levels are decreasing and rainfall intensity will remain too low to cause flooding problems
Now, before the storm arrives, because the forecast wind weakening does not mean the overall risk is lower — the historical pattern and forecast both show serious flooding is still coming inland

Not until after the storm passes inland, because the historical records describe only wind damage from past hurricanes and cannot provide reliable predictions about rainfall flooding in inland regions beyond the immediate coast

Only after the storm makes landfall and the wind damage phase is over, because rainfall flooding impacts cannot be forecast accurately until after forecasters observe actual storm intensity and track data from the landing itself
hints: A dropping wind category means what about the overall risk — is it automatically dropping too?
What two separate kinds of evidence both point toward the same inland flooding hazard?

problemText: A county experiences frequent flash flooding along a specific river, with historical records documenting that the river overflows a critical bridge whenever three-day rainfall totals exceed 8 inches. When that happens, floodwater moves fast across the roadway and is deeper than it appears from a car. The current forecast shows a storm system expected to deliver 6 inches of rain in the first two days, and meteorologists note uncertainty about whether additional rain will fall on the third day. The county proposes two possible actions: (1) Pre-close the bridge when the first 5 inches of rain has fallen, rerouting traffic immediately; (2) Wait until the actual rainfall total approaches 8 inches, then close the bridge if needed. Which action better fits the forecast data and historical evidence, and why?
choices: Action 2 is better, because the forecast only guarantees 6 inches of rain over the first two days, and waiting to measure the actual total before closing ensures the county does not overreact to uncertain forecasts
Action 2 is better, because closing the bridge too early wastes money on traffic rerouting, and the forecast does not guarantee that the third day's rain will actually occur

Action 1 is better, because the historical pattern shows a specific rainfall threshold tied to flooding, and the forecast includes uncertainty about a third day that could push the total to or above that threshold
Action 1 is better, because any rainfall over 5 inches is dangerous, and forecasts are always wrong by at least several inches, so erring on the side of caution is the only safe choice
hints: The historical record ties the bridge flooding to a specific number — what does that tell you about when to act?
Forecast uncertainty about a third day of rain — does that make it safer to wait until the full total is measured, or safer to act before the forecast uncertainty resolves?

problemText: A geologist uses the term 'elevated risk' to describe a coastal region that sits on an active convergent boundary where an oceanic plate is being forced beneath a continental plate. According to the hazard record, this region has experienced many earthquakes and volcanic eruptions over the past two hundred years. What does 'elevated risk' mean in this context?
choices: This region has a higher chance of earthquakes, eruptions, or tsunamis than a region with no active plate boundary nearby, but it does not predict when or whether a specific event will occur
A major earthquake or eruption is certain to happen in this region within the next few years based on the two-hundred-year pattern of activity, which guarantees the same sequence will repeat
The region's risk of future earthquakes decreases after each earthquake occurs because the collision process gradually slows down and stress relief reduces the likelihood of the next event
The past two hundred years of activity prove that this region will experience earthquakes at the exact same intervals in the next two hundred years with no variation in timing or magnitude
hints: Recall that elevated risk is based on a repeated pattern over time, not on certainty or prediction of a specific date.
Think about what 'elevated risk' compared to other regions means — it raises the odds, but does not guarantee or rule out when an event occurs.

problemText: A transform boundary, such as the San Andreas Fault in California, is characterized by two plates sliding past each other horizontally, with the distance between them staying roughly the same. The historical record for this region shows many earthquakes but no active volcanoes along the fault line itself. Based on what is known about different boundary types and their hazard patterns, which hazard should geologists expect to be most common at a transform boundary?
choices: Volcanic eruptions, because any plate boundary can generate enough heat to melt rock
Earthquakes, because the sliding motion of the two plates creates stress and sudden releases along the fault
Tsunamis, because transform boundaries always run along ocean coastlines where water can be displaced
Landslides, because the horizontal motion of the plates destabilizes all hillsides nearby
hints: Think about what happens when two plates slide past each other — what kind of motion creates stress and sudden movement?
Recall that volcanoes form where rock is being forced down and melted, or where new material is rising — neither happens at a transform boundary.

problemText: Two regions both sit on convergent boundaries. Region P has a long historical record of frequent earthquakes and active volcanoes arranged in a chain running parallel to the coast. Region Q, inland and far from any ocean, has the same pattern of frequent earthquakes but no active volcanoes at all. Both regions have repeatedly experienced strong earthquakes over the past three hundred years. Based on the hazard patterns described, what is the most likely difference between these two boundaries?
choices: Region P is at an oceanic-continental convergent boundary where magma is generated by subduction and rises to form a volcanic arc, while Region Q is at a continental-continental convergent boundary where the rocks are too thick and dense to melt easily
Region P experiences convergent motion while Region Q experiences divergent motion, even though both regions have strong earthquakes occurring
Region P's boundary involves an oceanic plate being subducted beneath a continental plate, while Region Q's boundary involves two continental plates colliding with each other
Region P's historical record is longer and more reliable than Region Q's record, which means volcanoes only appear in regions where scientists have kept detailed notes for centuries
hints: Recall that not every convergent boundary produces a volcanic arc — it depends on what type of plates are colliding.
Think about which combination of plates (oceanic and continental, or continental and continental) creates the conditions for a volcanic arc to form above a subduction zone.

problemText: A coastal research team surveys an underwater boundary and finds that an oceanic plate has been moving toward a continental plate for millions of years, with the distance between them steadily shrinking. Historical records from the past three hundred years show many strong earthquakes in the region and several volcanic eruptions. A colleague proposes that because the historical record shows these events have occurred repeatedly, a major earthquake is 'due' and is very likely to occur in the next five years. Is the colleague's conclusion justified by the evidence? Explain your reasoning using what the term 'elevated risk' actually means.
choices: Yes, because a pattern of repeated earthquakes over three hundred years means another one is statistically guaranteed to occur within exactly five years based on the average time between events
No, because convergent boundaries produce earthquakes so massive that they destroy all historical records, making it impossible to use past data to determine when the next earthquake is overdue

Yes, because earthquakes and volcanic eruptions follow predictable cycles that repeat on a fixed schedule, so the three-hundred-year record allows precise forecasting of when the next major event will strike

No, because elevated risk describes a higher-than-average chance based on the boundary type and past pattern, not a prediction of when the next event will happen; the boundary's presence makes future hazards more likely than in a stable region, but does not determine a specific year
hints: In science, elevated risk means a higher-than-average probability compared to other regions, not a guaranteed event in a specific timeframe — think about what information a plate boundary actually gives us.
Consider what the presence of a plate boundary tells us — it raises the probability compared to other regions, but what does it NOT tell us?

problemText: A geologist studies two regions and gathers the following information: Region M sits on the coast, where an oceanic plate meets a continental plate at a convergent boundary, and has experienced many earthquakes and several volcanic eruptions over the past two hundred years. Region N sits hundreds of kilometers inland, also on a convergent boundary where two continental plates are colliding, and has experienced many earthquakes but no volcanic eruptions in the same time period. Based on the boundary types and geographic settings, which region carries an elevated risk of tsunami hazards, and why?
choices: Region M, because a coastal boundary where an oceanic plate is subducted can produce earthquakes that suddenly shift the seafloor and displace the ocean water above it; Region N's inland location means there is no ocean above its boundary to be displaced
Region N, because inland convergent boundaries produce much stronger earthquakes than coastal boundaries and generate larger ocean waves that travel farther inland to affect populated areas
Both regions equally, because any convergent boundary with a history of strong earthquakes over two hundred years will eventually produce a tsunami regardless of coastal or inland location
Neither region, because tsunamis only form from volcanic eruptions beneath the ocean surface, and earthquakes occurring at plate boundaries cannot displace enough water to create hazardous waves
hints: Think about what is required for a tsunami to form — what must be displaced, and does every region have that?
Recall that location matters: a coastal boundary and an inland boundary are both convergent, but they carry different hazard mixes because of what sits above or below them.

problemText: A team of geologists discovers a region with the following characteristics: (1) The region sits on the coast. (2) Surveys using the Unit 4 method show that an oceanic plate has been steadily closing the distance with a continental plate for millions of years. (3) The historical record spanning five hundred years shows frequent earthquakes and many volcanic eruptions. (4) A large earthquake struck this region seventy years ago. A government official claims that because seventy years have passed since the last major earthquake, the region is now 'safer' and carries less elevated risk than it did before the last earthquake. Using your understanding of what causes elevated risk, explain whether the official's claim is correct.
choices: The official is correct — after a major earthquake releases stress at the plate boundary, the risk of future earthquakes drops significantly until stress builds back up over many decades

The official is incorrect — elevated risk is based on the plate boundary type and the long-term historical pattern, not on when the last event happened; the boundary itself has not changed or become inactive, so the risk remains elevated

The official is correct — geological patterns show that major earthquakes at the same boundary require at least one hundred years to rebuild enough stress for the next major event, making seventy years a safe period

The official is incorrect — regions that experience earthquakes become progressively more dangerous over time, so the passage of seventy years without an earthquake means stress has been building and the region is now more hazardous than it was immediately after the last earthquake
hints: Think about what 'elevated risk' is based on — is it the timing of the last event, or is it something more permanent that characterizes the location?
Consider whether a plate boundary changes or 'goes away' after an earthquake occurs. If the boundary is still there, does the source of the hazard still exist?
